reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A milder FGFR3-related skeletal dysplasia that phenotypically resembles a subtle form of achondroplasia and is often not recognised until mid-childhood
Features include mildly disproportionate short stature with predominantly rhizomelic to mesomelic limb shortening, stocky build, and mild lumbar lordosis
Craniofacial features are much less marked than in achondroplasia, and macrocephaly and frontal bossing are mild or absent
Caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in FGFR3, distinct from and generally milder than the achondroplasia variant
Radiographs show mild long-bone shortening, squared ilia, and characteristically failure of the lumbar interpedicular distance to widen caudally, though changes can be subtle
A proportion of patients have learning difficulties or epilepsy, particularly those with certain variants
Confirmation is by FGFR3 molecular testing, as radiographic and clinical overlap with normal variation and other dysplasias can be considerable
reference.pathophysiology: Hypochondroplasia results from activating variants in FGFR3, the same receptor implicated in achondroplasia, but the substitutions produce a lesser degree of constitutive signalling. Excess FGFR3 activity again inhibits growth-plate chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification, but the milder biochemical effect yields a correspondingly milder skeletal phenotype with less pronounced disproportion and craniofacial change than achondroplasia.
additionalDifferentials: SHOX-related short stature and Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey looking for the lumbar interpedicular pattern, squared ilia, and mild long-bone shortening
FGFR3 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and distinguish from achondroplasia
Assessment of body proportions and serial growth charting
SHOX gene testing when disproportion is predominantly mesomelic and FGFR3 testing is negative
Neurodevelopmental assessment where learning difficulty or seizures are present
Spinal imaging if symptomatic canal narrowing is suspected in adulthood
redFlags: Seizures or developmental regression prompting neuroimaging and neurology review
Symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis in adulthood
Disproportion more severe than expected, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have a normal lifespan and only mild reduction in adult height, functioning well without major complications. A minority experience learning difficulties, epilepsy, or symptomatic spinal stenosis in later life.
pitfalls: Dismissing the diagnosis because features are mild, leading to delayed recognition
Confusing it with achondroplasia given the shared gene and overlapping appearance
Failing to consider SHOX-related conditions in the differential of mild disproportion
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
